context.heading: Proof that settles the case
context.body: Luke says Jesus presented Himself alive with many tekmēria ("convincing proofs"). Aristotle used the word for decisive evidence that settles a question. Luke promised Theophilus certainty (Luke 1:3–4), so he grounds Acts in forty days of seeing, hearing and even eating with the risen Jesus.

context.heading: A question about restoring Israel
context.body: The disciples ask if Jesus will now apokathistēmi ("restore") the kingdom to Israel. The Greek Old Testament uses this verb for Elijah's future work of restoring things before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:6; compare Mark 9:12). Jesus does not call their hope foolish. He redirects it: the timing is the Father's, and the scope is wider than they imagine.

context.heading: Why cast lots?
context.body: The believers cast klēroi ("lots"), probably marked stones shaken in a container until one fell out. Israel used lots to divide the land and assign priestly duties (Numbers 26:55; 1 Chronicles 24:5; Luke 1:9), trusting that "its every decision is from the LORD" (Proverbs 16:33). After Pentecost the New Testament never records lots used this way again.

theology.title: The King takes His throne
theology.body: A cloud hides Jesus as He is taken up (v. 9), the kind of cloud that marks God's presence (Exodus 40:34; Luke 9:34). Daniel saw one like a son of man come with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receive an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14). The ascension is not Jesus leaving the story but Jesus being enthroned. The angels promise He will come back the same way (v. 11).

theology.title: The Father keeps His promise
theology.body: Jesus tells the disciples to wait for "the gift the Father promised" (v. 4), the Spirit foretold by the prophets and by John the Baptist (v. 5). The times and dates belong to the Father's authority (v. 7). That is a comfort: the God who sets the calendar is the God who keeps His word.

theology.title: Even betrayal cannot derail Him
theology.body: Peter says Scripture "had to be fulfilled" about Judas (v. 16), quoting Psalms 69:25 and 109:8. Judas acted freely and wickedly, yet God was not caught off guard. Choosing Matthias restores the Twelve, a number tied to Israel's twelve tribes (Luke 22:30). God is renewing His people, not giving up on them.

application.title: Waiting is not wasted
application.body: Jesus hands His followers a world-sized mission and then tells them to wait. They spend those days praying together, not drawing up plans. Before your next big push at work, church or home, the hardest step may be to stop and depend on God first.
application.question: What are you charging ahead on right now that you have never honestly brought to God?

application.title: Witnesses, not salespeople
application.body: A witness tells what they have seen and heard; they do not need to win every argument. Jesus says "you will be My witnesses," which describes who you are before it describes a task. Your coworkers need an honest account of what Jesus has done in you more than a polished presentation.
application.question: If a friend asked what difference Jesus has made in your life this year, what would you actually say?

application.title: Stop staring at the sky
application.body: The angels' question carries a hint of humor: why stand there looking up? Fascination with end-time timelines can become a way to dodge the plain obedience in front of us. Jesus answered the disciples' "When?" with "Go."
application.question: Which question about the future gets more of your energy than the next step Jesus has plainly given you?

context.heading: A harvest feast fifty days after Passover
context.body: Pentecost (Greek pentēkostē, "fiftieth") is the Feast of Weeks, held fifty days after Passover (Leviticus 23:15–21; Deuteronomy 16:9–12). It was one of three feasts when Jewish men were expected in Jerusalem, and it thanked God for the firstfruits of the wheat harvest. Luke's timing is pointed: fifty days after Jesus died at Passover, about three thousand people are gathered in as the first harvest of the church. Later Jewish writers also tied the feast to the giving of the law at Sinai, and many readers hear echoes of Sinai's fire and loud sound (Exodus 19:16–19) in this chapter.

context.heading: Wind, breath and Spirit
context.body: The sound is like a mighty rushing wind (pnoē, "breath" or "blast"). In Greek, pneuma means wind, breath and spirit, as Hebrew ruach does, so the sign fits what it announces. Readers who knew the Scriptures would think of God breathing life into Adam (Genesis 2:7), the wind blowing life into dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9–14) and Jesus' words that the Spirit blows like the wind (John 3:8).

context.heading: Fire that rests on each one
context.body: Fire often marks God's presence in the Old Testament: the burning bush, the pillar of fire, Sinai, and the fire that fell on the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 3:2; 40:38; 2 Chronicles 7:1). John the Baptist promised that the coming one would baptize "with the Holy Spirit and with fire" (Luke 3:16). Here the fire separates and rests on each believer. God's presence is no longer centered on one building but dwells in His people.

context.heading: Real languages the visitors understood
context.body: The crowd hears the disciples in their own dialektos, their native language or dialect (vv. 6, 8). Luke stresses that these were known languages, since visitors from many lands understood them without an interpreter. Many readers see this as a reversal of Babel, where God scattered the nations by confusing their language (Genesis 11:1–9). At Pentecost the nations hear one message, each in its own tongue.

context.heading: Pilgrims from every nation under heaven
context.body: The list runs roughly from Parthia in the east to Rome in the west, with Arabia and Crete at the edges. These were mostly Jews of the dispersion, scattered since the exiles, along with proselytes (Gentiles who had converted to Judaism). The list echoes the table of nations in Genesis 10 and previews the gospel going "to the ends of the earth" (Acts 1:8). Some who believed would carry the message home.

context.heading: Joel and the last days
context.body: Peter quotes Joel 2:28–32 and opens it with "in the last days" (eschatos). In the New Testament the last days are the whole age that began with Jesus' resurrection and the Spirit's coming and runs until He returns (Hebrews 1:2). Under the old covenant the Spirit came on chosen prophets, kings and craftsmen. Joel promised the Spirit for sons and daughters, young and old, and even servants, and Peter says that day has come. The cosmic signs in vv. 19–20 use prophetic language for God's coming judgment; Christians read them in different ways, some as fulfilled in part at the cross and Pentecost and some as still to come.

context.heading: David's tomb was still there
context.body: Peter's crowd could walk to David's tomb (mnēma) in Jerusalem; the historian Josephus also mentions it. That is the point of Peter's argument from Psalm 16. David wrote, "You will not let Your Holy One see decay," yet David died and his body decayed. So the psalm must speak of the Messiah, David's descendant, whom God raised. Peter then cites Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes most often, to show the Messiah would be enthroned at God's right hand.

context.heading: Cut to the heart
context.body: Katanyssō means to pierce or stab sharply. The crowd realizes that the Jesus they rejected weeks earlier is the Lord and Christ (v. 36). Their question, "What shall we do?", shows that the sermon pierced their conscience and did not only inform them. Peter's answer is immediate: repent, be baptized in Jesus' name, and receive the promised Spirit.

context.heading: Devoted to four things
context.body: Proskartereō means to hold fast, persist and keep at something. The same word describes the disciples praying together before Pentecost (Acts 1:14) and meeting daily in the temple (v. 46). The new believers keep at the apostles' teaching, fellowship (koinōnia), the breaking of bread and the prayers. They still went to the temple, since the first Christians were Jews who saw Jesus as the fulfillment of their faith, and they also met in homes.

theology.title: The promise of the Spirit kept
theology.body: Pentecost fulfills what God promised through the prophets (Joel 2:28; Ezekiel 36:26–27) and what Jesus promised His disciples (Luke 24:49; John 14:16–17; Acts 1:4–5). The Spirit had been at work before, but now He is poured out on all God's people to dwell in them and empower their witness. The chapter is also quietly Trinitarian: the Son, exalted to the Father's right hand, receives the promised Spirit from the Father and pours Him out (v. 33).

theology.title: Jesus is Lord and Christ
theology.body: Peter's sermon is about Jesus, not the tongues. God attested Him by miracles (v. 22), God raised Him (vv. 24, 32) and God exalted Him (v. 33), so "God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ" (v. 36). In v. 21 Joel's "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord" refers to the LORD, Israel's God. By v. 38 people are baptized in the name of Jesus. The earliest Christian preaching already gives Jesus the name and honor that belong to God.

theology.title: God's plan and human responsibility
theology.body: Jesus was handed over "by God's set plan and foreknowledge," and He was also put to death by lawless hands (v. 23). Scripture holds both together without explaining away either. God's purpose stood behind the cross, and the people who rejected Jesus were truly guilty, which is why they are called to repent. The worst thing humans ever did became the means of their salvation.

theology.title: Repentance, faith and baptism
theology.body: Peter calls for repentance, a turning of the whole life, and baptism in Jesus' name, with the promise of forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit (v. 38). Christians understand how baptism relates to forgiveness in different ways. Many evangelicals see baptism as the public sign of a faith that has already received forgiveness, pointing to passages that tie forgiveness to faith alone (Acts 10:43; 16:31). Other traditions see baptism as a means God uses to give grace. All agree the call is to turn to Christ and be joined to His people, and the promise reaches "all who are far off" (v. 39).

theology.title: Tongues and Spirit baptism: where Christians differ
theology.body: Believers read Pentecost differently. Pentecostal and many charismatic Christians see baptism in the Spirit as an experience distinct from conversion, often marked by speaking in tongues, and expect it today. Many other evangelicals hold that every believer is baptized by the Spirit at conversion (1 Corinthians 12:13). They see Pentecost as a one-time turning point in God's plan, like the cross and resurrection, rather than a pattern each Christian repeats. Christians also differ on whether tongues continue today. Common ground: every believer receives the Spirit (v. 38), and the Spirit's work points to Jesus.

theology.title: A new community
theology.body: The Spirit creates a people as well as changing individuals. The first believers learn from the apostles, share life, eat together, pray, give to anyone in need and worship with glad hearts (vv. 42–47). The sharing was voluntary love, not a required economic system; Acts 5:4 notes that property remained the owner's to keep or give. Luke presents it as a picture of what the Spirit does when He fills a church.

application.title: The Spirit is for ordinary believers
application.body: Joel's promise includes sons and daughters, young and old, and servants. God's Spirit is given to every believer, not only to leaders or especially gifted people. Your faith is meant to be lived in His power, not only your own effort.
application.question: Where have you assumed God works through other people but not through you?

application.title: Let Scripture interpret experience
application.body: Something astonishing happened, and Peter explained it from Joel and the Psalms. He did not build his message on the experience itself. Strong spiritual moments are good gifts, and the Bible tells us what they mean and tests whether they are from God.
application.question: When something stirs you spiritually, how do you weigh it against Scripture?

application.title: Conviction calls for a response
application.body: The crowd was cut to the heart and asked, "What shall we do?" Conviction is God's kindness when it leads us to act. It is not meant to leave us feeling guilty and stuck.
application.question: Is there something God has been pressing on your heart that needs a clear step of obedience this week?

application.title: Keep at the basics
application.body: The first church kept at four simple things: the apostles' teaching (Scripture), fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer. Spiritual growth comes from steadily practicing these in the company of other believers.
application.question: Which of the four is thinnest in your life right now, and what is one small step to strengthen it?

application.title: Generosity that notices need
application.body: The believers gave to anyone as they had need. The Spirit made them notice one another. Generosity is one of the clearest signs that a church has been changed by the gospel.
application.question: Whose need around you could you help meet this week?

context.heading: Echoes of Isaiah's Servant
context.body: Peter says God "has glorified His servant (pais) Jesus." In the Greek Old Testament, Isaiah 52:13 says God's Servant will be lifted up and greatly glorified, just before the song of the Servant who suffers for the sins of others (Isaiah 53). Pais can mean "child" or "servant." The early church kept using it of Jesus in prayer (Acts 4:27, 30).

context.heading: Wholeness in full view
context.body: The man stands before everyone in holoklēria ("complete health"), a word for something sound in every part. He had been lame for more than forty years (4:22) and was a familiar sight at the gate, so no one could claim the healing was staged. Peter insists the power is not his own; it comes through faith in Jesus' name (vv. 12, 16).

context.heading: Refreshing now, restoration later
context.body: Peter speaks of "times of refreshing" from the Lord and of a coming apokatastasis ("restoration") of all things, as God promised through the prophets. It is the noun form of the verb the disciples used in 1:6. Israel's hope for a renewed world has not been cancelled. It waits for Jesus to return from heaven.

theology.title: The God of Abraham raised Jesus
theology.body: Peter calls God "the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers" (v. 13), the name God gave Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:6, 15). The God who called the patriarchs and rescued Israel from Egypt is the one who raised Jesus. There is no new God here, only old promises reaching their goal.

theology.title: The prophet like Moses
theology.body: Peter quotes Deuteronomy 18:15–19: God would raise up a prophet like Moses, and everyone must listen to Him. In Jesus' day many watched for this Prophet (John 1:21; 6:14). Peter says Jesus is that Prophet, and that every prophet from Samuel onward pointed to these days (v. 24).

theology.title: Blessing for every family
theology.body: Peter closes with God's promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through his offspring (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). God sent His Servant "first" to Israel, to bless them by turning each of them from their wicked ways (v. 26). That small word "first" hints at what Acts will show: the blessing is headed for the nations too.

application.title: Give what you do have
application.body: Peter had no silver or gold, so he gave what he had. We often hold back because we lack money, expertise or the right words. The man at the gate needed something deeper than coins, and so do most people we walk past.
application.question: Whom have you been avoiding because you assumed you had nothing to offer them?

application.title: Redirect the stares
application.body: When the crowd gapes at Peter and John, Peter asks why they are looking at the apostles at all. Praise, success and a growing platform tempt every believer to keep a little of the glory. Peter points straight past himself to Jesus.
application.question: When people praise you, where do your next words point their attention?

application.title: Ignorance explains but does not erase
application.body: Peter grants that the crowd acted in ignorance, and he still calls them to repent. Not knowing better explains sin, but only God can wipe it away. That is sobering and freeing at once.
application.question: What have you excused with "I didn't know" that you now need to bring honestly to God?

context.heading: Untrained, not illiterate
context.body: The council sees Peter and John as agrammatoi and idiōtai. Agrammatos literally means "without letters," but here it most likely means without formal training in the law, not unable to read. Idiōtēs meant a layman, an amateur rather than a professional. The leaders cannot explain how fishermen argue from Scripture like scholars, and they trace it to time spent with Jesus.

context.heading: Why the Sadducees were angry
context.body: The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple, and they denied any resurrection of the dead (23:8). Now apostles were announcing in the temple courts that Jesus had risen. The message attacked both their theology and their authority on their own ground.

context.heading: Praying to the Master of all
context.body: The church addresses God as despotēs ("Sovereign Lord"), a word for a master with full authority over a household, the source of English "despot." Under threat, they start with who God is: maker of heaven, earth and sea. Simeon used the same title when he held the infant Jesus (Luke 2:29).

theology.title: The rejected stone
theology.body: Peter tells Israel's leaders that Jesus is the stone the builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone (Psalm 118:22). He says it to the builders themselves. Jesus had quoted the same psalm against these leaders (Luke 20:17), and Peter returns to it in his letter (1 Peter 2:7). God builds His house on the one people threw away.

theology.title: God rules over the rulers
theology.body: The church reads Psalm 2 as a description of recent events: nations and rulers raging against the Lord and His Anointed (vv. 25–26). Herod, Pilate, Gentiles and Israel joined forces, yet they did only what God's hand and purpose had decided beforehand (v. 28). God's sovereignty does not make evil less evil. It means evil never gets the last word.

theology.title: Filled again for a new task
theology.body: The meeting place shakes and they are all filled with the Holy Spirit (v. 31), though many had been filled at Pentecost. In Acts the Spirit's filling can happen repeatedly, often for bold speech in a hard moment (4:8; 13:9). Christians describe how this relates to Spirit baptism in different ways. All agree God gives fresh strength for each new demand.

application.title: Time with Jesus shows
application.body: The council could not explain Peter and John by their credentials. What marked them was time spent with Jesus. Your lack of qualifications matters less than you fear, and the character formed in you shows more than you think.
application.question: If someone watched you closely for a week, what would they conclude about whom you spend time with?

application.title: Pray bigger than the threat
application.body: Threatened by the most powerful men in their nation, the believers did not ask for safety. They asked for boldness and for God to keep working. Our prayers often shrink to comfort when the real need is courage.
application.question: What would change if you asked for courage in the situation you have only been asking God to remove?

application.title: An open hand with real things
application.body: No one called their possessions their own, and Barnabas sold a field and gave the money. This was voluntary, but it was real property let go by a real man. Generosity is less a feeling than a specific thing released.
application.question: What do you own that you would struggle to call God's if someone near you needed it?

context.heading: An echo of Achan
context.body: Ananias "kept back" part of the money; the verb is nosphizō, "to embezzle" or "pilfer." The Greek Old Testament uses the same rare word for Achan, who secretly took devoted goods at Jericho and brought judgment on Israel (Joshua 7:1). As Israel was entering the land then, God's people are just beginning now. The sin was not keeping money, which was his right (v. 4), but lying about it.

context.heading: The first church in Acts
context.body: Great fear comes over the whole ekklēsia ("church" or "assembly"), the first time most translations of Acts use the word for the believers. In the Greek Old Testament it often names Israel gathered before God, as at Sinai (Deuteronomy 4:10). Luke introduces it right after a story about God's holiness among His people.

context.heading: Who was Gamaliel?
context.body: Gamaliel was one of the most respected Pharisee teachers of his day, honored in later Jewish tradition as Rabban Gamaliel the Elder and named as Paul's teacher (22:3). He cites failed movements led by Theudas and Judas the Galilean. His wait-and-see advice is wise as far as it goes, but Luke's readers already know this movement is from God.

theology.title: A holy God among His people
theology.body: The deaths of Ananias and Sapphira recall Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10:1–2) and Achan (Joshua 7), sudden judgments at the start of a new chapter in God's dwelling with His people. God's presence is a gift, but it is never tame. The same Spirit who heals and fills cannot be deceived, and the church learns fear and joy together.

theology.title: Freed to go back
theology.body: An angel opens the jail and sends the apostles straight back to the temple to tell the people "the full message of this new life" (v. 20). God rescues them not for a quiet escape but for renewed witness in the same place. Jesus, exalted as Prince and Savior, gives Israel repentance and forgiveness (v. 31). Even repentance is His gift.

theology.title: Honor in dishonor
theology.body: The apostles leave the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer disgrace for the Name (v. 41). "The Name" stands for Jesus Himself, the way devout Jews spoke reverently of God's name. Jesus had said those insulted for Him are blessed (Luke 6:22–23). The apostles take Him at His word.

application.title: Generosity for an audience
application.body: Ananias did not have to give anything, since the land was his. His sin was wanting credit for a sacrifice he had not made. Social media offers the same temptation daily: a curated image of devotion that private life does not match.
application.question: Where are you letting people believe something about your faith or giving that is not quite true?

application.title: Defiance without disrespect
application.body: The apostles refuse the council's order, yet they do not riot, insult or run. They state their reason plainly and accept the beating. Obeying God over people, in Scripture, is narrow, costly and clear about why.
application.question: Where are you treating a preference as a matter of conscience, or a matter of conscience as a mere preference?

application.title: Joy that makes no sense
application.body: Freshly flogged, the apostles go home rejoicing. Their joy came from whose name they carried, not from comfort. Being the odd one out for your faith at work or school is a small version of what they faced.
application.question: What would it look like to treat your next awkward moment for Jesus as an honor instead of a loss?

context.heading: Grumbling with a long history
context.body: The complaint is a gongysmos, a "murmuring" or "grumbling," a word that almost sounds like what it means. The Greek Old Testament uses it for Israel grumbling against Moses and God in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7–9). Luke's word choice quietly warns that this kind of division is an old danger among God's people.

context.heading: Two kinds of Jewish believers
context.body: The Hellēnistai were Jews whose first language was Greek, many of them born outside Judea and used to reading Scripture in Greek. The "Hebrews" spoke Aramaic and were mostly local. Some scholars suggest many widows had moved to Jerusalem late in life, far from extended family, which would leave them dependent on the community's daily support.

context.heading: The Synagogue of the Freedmen
context.body: Stephen's opponents come from the Synagogue of the Freedmen, probably descendants of Jews once taken to Rome as slaves and later freed. A first-century inscription found in Jerusalem, the Theodotus inscription, describes a Greek-speaking synagogue built for reading the law and housing visitors from abroad. Stephen's fiercest opponents were Greek-speaking Jews like himself.

theology.title: God defends the widow
theology.body: Throughout Scripture God is the defender of widows, orphans and foreigners (Deuteronomy 10:18; Psalm 68:5; James 1:27). A food line for widows is not a side issue but a reflection of God's own character. The apostles do not wave the complaint away; they meet it with structure and Spirit-filled people.

theology.title: The word keeps growing
theology.body: Once the problem is solved, Luke reports that the word of God spread and many priests became obedient to the faith (v. 7). This is one of several progress reports in Acts (12:24; 19:20), where God's word grows almost like a living thing. Even good administration serves that growth. Priests believing shows the gospel reaching the heart of the temple system.

theology.title: Charged like his Lord
theology.body: Stephen is accused of saying Jesus would destroy the temple and change the customs of Moses (vv. 13–14). The charge echoes the false witnesses at Jesus' own trial (Mark 14:57–58), who also twisted real words. Jesus had spoken of a new temple, His own body (John 2:19–21). Stephen grasped that God's presence was not locked in one building.

application.title: Complaints can carry truth
application.body: The Greek-speaking widows really were being overlooked. The apostles listened and acted instead of defending themselves. A complaint in a family, workplace or church may be pointing at a real blind spot.
application.question: What recurring complaint around you might be telling you something true that you have not wanted to hear?

application.title: No task too small for the Spirit
application.body: The men chosen to run a food program had to be full of the Spirit and wisdom. One of them, Stephen, became a powerful preacher and the church's first martyr. Serving tables was not a lesser calling than preaching.
application.question: Which part of your work have you decided does not need God's help or your best effort?

application.title: Hand power to the overlooked
application.body: All seven men chosen had Greek names, so they likely came from the very group that felt neglected. The church did not just patch the problem; it gave authority to those affected. That takes humility from the people in charge.
application.question: Where could you share decisions with the people most affected by them?

context.heading: Israel's assembly in the desert
context.body: Stephen calls Israel in the wilderness the ekklēsia ("congregation" or "assembly"), the same word Luke uses for the church. The link is deliberate. Moses led an assembly that received "living words" at Sinai and then turned away to a golden calf. Stephen implies that God's true people are those who listen to the prophet like Moses (v. 37).

context.heading: A neck that will not bend
context.body: Sklērotrachēlos ("stiff-necked") pictures an ox that refuses to bow its neck to the yoke. God used the word of Israel after the golden calf (Exodus 33:3, 5), and "uncircumcised hearts" comes from Leviticus 26:41 and Jeremiah 9:26. Stephen turns Moses' own vocabulary on the men who claim to defend Moses.

context.heading: Why is Jesus standing?
context.body: Elsewhere Jesus is pictured seated at God's right hand (Psalm 110:1; Luke 22:69), but Stephen sees Him standing. Some interpreters think He rises to welcome His servant. Others see Him standing as a witness in heaven's court while an earthly court condemns Stephen. Either way, Jesus is acknowledging before God the man who acknowledged Him before people (Luke 12:8).

theology.title: The God who goes with His people
theology.body: Stephen's history keeps finding God outside the land: appearing to Abraham in Mesopotamia (v. 2), staying with Joseph in Egypt (v. 9), and making desert ground holy at the burning bush (v. 33). Solomon himself confessed that heaven cannot contain God (1 Kings 8:27). God's presence goes where His people go, which prepares for the gospel's move beyond Jerusalem.

theology.title: Deliverers rejected, then vindicated
theology.body: Joseph was rejected by his brothers, and Moses by the Israelite who asked, "Who made you ruler and judge over us?" (v. 27). Yet both were the deliverers God sent. Stephen traces the pattern to its climax: the Righteous One, betrayed and murdered (v. 52). God has repeatedly saved His people through the one they refused.

theology.title: A prayer answered later
theology.body: Luke notes a young man named Saul guarding the coats (v. 58). The stoning looks like defeat, yet Stephen's plea for his killers is answered in a way no one there could imagine. An old saying, often credited to Augustine, holds that the church owes Paul to Stephen's prayer. God works through what looks like loss.

application.title: Know the story, not just verses
application.body: Stephen, a man chosen to serve tables, answered the highest court in the land by retelling Israel's history from memory. He knew the Bible as one story leading to Jesus. That kind of knowledge is built over years of steady reading.
application.question: Could you explain to a curious friend, in five minutes, how the Old Testament leads to Jesus?

application.title: Devout and still resistant
application.body: Stephen's hearers honored Scripture and the temple, yet they resisted the Spirit. Being religious is not the same as being teachable. Resistance often dresses itself as loyalty to tradition.
application.question: Where might your loyalty to how things have always been done be resisting something God is doing?

application.title: Forgive while it still hurts
application.body: Stephen prays for his killers while the stones are still flying. Forgiveness here is not a feeling that arrives later but a choice made in pain. That prayer reached at least one man in the crowd.
application.question: Who could you pray a blessing over today, even though the hurt is still fresh?

context.heading: Magic was a business
context.body: Simon had been mageuōn ("practicing magic"), and the crowds called him "the Great Power" (v. 10). Ancient magic was a trade, selling spells for love, health, revenge and protection from spirits. Simon sees the apostles' power as a better product. Later church writers made him the father of heresies, though those stories are hard to verify.

context.heading: Poison at the root
context.body: Peter says Simon is "in the gall (cholē) of bitterness." Gall was bitter bile or a poisonous herb. The phrase echoes Deuteronomy 29:18, which warns of a root among God's people bearing poison and bitterness: someone who hears the covenant yet keeps his own way. Simon's attempt to buy power gave us the word "simony," the buying of church office.

context.heading: Treasurer to a queen of Kush
context.body: Candace was not a personal name but a royal title for the queen mother of Kush, the kingdom south of Egypt in today's Sudan, centered at Meroë. Greeks and Romans called the region Ethiopia and thought of it as the edge of the world. A senior official from there believing in Jesus is a first step toward "the ends of the earth" (1:8).

theology.title: Mending an old division
theology.body: Jews and Samaritans had been divided for centuries over ancestry, temple and worship (John 4:9, 20). By giving the Spirit to the Samaritan believers through Peter and John, God binds them to the Jerusalem church instead of creating a rival one. Christians explain the delay in different ways, but its result is one people, not two.

theology.title: Starting from Isaiah 53
theology.body: The official is reading about the Servant led like a sheep to slaughter and denied justice (Isaiah 53:7–8). Philip begins with that very Scripture and tells him about Jesus (v. 35). Jesus had taught that all the Scriptures speak of Him (Luke 24:27). The suffering Servant is the key that unlocks the passage and the reader's heart.

theology.title: A gift that cannot be bought
theology.body: Simon treats the Spirit as a power to acquire and resell. Peter answers that God's gift cannot be obtained with money (v. 20). The Spirit is a person and a gift, not a technique. Grace that could be purchased would no longer be grace.

application.title: Scattered, not stopped
application.body: The believers fled their homes and kept talking about Jesus wherever they landed. A move, a layoff or a collapsed plan can feel like being thrown out. It may be God placing you somewhere new on purpose.
application.question: What unwanted change in your life might God be using to put you near people who need Him?

application.title: Faith as leverage
application.body: Simon wanted the Spirit's power for his career. The same impulse shows up when faith becomes a platform, a brand or a way to build business contacts. God will not be leveraged.
application.question: What do you hope to get out of God that you have not admitted even to yourself?

application.title: Admit what you don't know
application.body: The official was not embarrassed to ask, "How can I, unless someone guides me?" Many people stay stuck because they will not admit confusion. Philip was ready because he ran toward the chariot.
application.question: What part of the Bible have you quietly given up on understanding, and who could help you with it?

context.heading: Every breath a threat
context.body: Saul was still empneōn, "breathing," threats and murder. The picture is of someone whose every breath is hostility, as if rage were the air he lived on. Damascus had a large Jewish community, and letters from the high priest carried weight with its synagogues. Saul planned to bring believers back to Jerusalem in chains.

context.heading: Hunter and hunted
context.body: Jesus asks, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute (diōkeis) Me?" The verb means to pursue or hunt down, as one chases a fleeing enemy. Saul thought he was hunting heretics; Jesus says he was hunting Him. Later Paul uses the same verb for pressing on to take hold of Christ (Philippians 3:12, 14). The hunter's energy is redirected.

context.heading: A woman called Gazelle
context.body: Tabitha in Aramaic and Dorcas in Greek both mean "gazelle," fitting for Joppa, a port with a mixed population. The widows show Peter the tunics she had made (v. 39), evidence of practical love. Peter's command, "Tabitha, get up," closely echoes Jesus' "Talitha koum" (Mark 5:41). The apostle does what his Lord did, in his Lord's power.

theology.title: Grace that seizes an enemy
theology.body: Saul did not go looking for Jesus; Jesus stopped him on the road. Paul later points to his conversion as proof of Christ's patience: if He saved the worst of sinners, He can save anyone (1 Timothy 1:15–16). Christians differ on how God's call and human response fit together, but here the initiative is plainly God's.

theology.title: The glory has a name
theology.body: A blinding light from heaven, a voice and a man thrown to the ground recall Old Testament visions of God's glory, as when Ezekiel fell facedown (Ezekiel 1:28). Saul asks, "Who are You, Lord?" The answer is, "I am Jesus." The glory Saul knew from Scripture has a face and a name.

theology.title: Chosen to suffer
theology.body: The Lord tells Ananias, "I will show him how much he must suffer for My name" (v. 16). Saul's calling is costly from the first day, and plots against him follow in Damascus and Jerusalem (vv. 23, 29). In Scripture, being chosen by God and suffering for Him often go together (2 Corinthians 11:23–28).

application.title: The Ananias moment
application.body: Ananias had good reason to avoid Saul, whose reputation was real and dangerous. He went anyway, and his first words were "Brother Saul." Sometimes obedience means walking toward the person you most fear or resent.
application.question: Who is the person you would least want God to ask you to welcome?

application.title: Be someone's Barnabas
application.body: The Jerusalem disciples were afraid of Saul and kept their distance. Barnabas brought him to the apostles and vouched for him. People with messy pasts often need a sponsor more than a sermon.
application.question: Who is still on the outside at your church, and what would it take for you to vouch for them?

application.title: Remembered for tunics
application.body: Dorcas was known for sewing clothes and helping the poor, and a room full of widows wept for her. Her ministry was ordinary and hands-on. Unseen kindness is not small to God.
application.question: What would the people closest to you hold up as evidence of your love?

context.heading: A Roman officer in Herod's city
context.body: Cornelius is a centurion in the Italian speira ("Regiment" or "cohort"), a unit of several hundred soldiers. Inscriptions mention an Italian cohort of Roman citizens stationed in Syria in the first century. Caesarea was Rome's seat of government in Judea, a showpiece port built by Herod the Great with a temple to Augustus.

context.heading: A God-fearing Gentile
context.body: Cornelius is devout and "feared (phoboumenos) God." Luke uses the phrase for Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God, attended synagogue and gave to the poor, but had not become full converts through circumcision (13:16, 26). Cornelius keeps the Jewish hour of prayer at three in the afternoon (v. 3; 3:1). He was close to Israel's faith yet still an outsider.

context.heading: Why Peter hesitated
context.body: Peter says it is athemitos ("unlawful" or "taboo") for a Jew to associate with a Gentile. The Law of Moses did not directly forbid it, but strict custom avoided Gentile homes and meals because of purity and food laws. Peter is already lodging with a tanner (9:43), whose work with dead animals many Jews considered unclean.

theology.title: Lord of all
theology.body: Peter's summary of the gospel includes a short phrase with large meaning: Jesus Christ "is Lord of all" (v. 36). God anointed Him with the Spirit and power (v. 38), as Isaiah 61:1 foretold, and appointed Him judge of the living and the dead (v. 42). If He is Lord of all, His peace is offered to all.

theology.title: God works both ends
theology.body: An angel visits Cornelius, a vision prepares Peter, and the Spirit tells Peter to go (v. 19). Peter arrives to find a house already gathered and waiting to hear (vv. 24, 33). The God who promised Abraham that all nations would be blessed (Genesis 12:3) arranges the meeting down to the timing of a lunch break.

theology.title: Gentiles receive the same Spirit
theology.body: The Spirit falls on Cornelius's household before they are baptized and before Peter has finished speaking (v. 44). The Jewish believers are astonished that the gift came "even on the Gentiles" (v. 45). Christians draw different lessons about the order of faith, Spirit and baptism here. The central point is clear: God accepts Gentiles on the same footing, by faith (v. 43; 15:8–9).

application.title: Even apostles get corrected
application.body: Peter argued with God: "No, Lord!" Long-held convictions can be wrong at the edges, even in faithful people. God corrected Peter through a vision and then through a real encounter with a person.
application.question: Which group of people have you quietly decided God is less interested in?

application.title: Walk through the door
application.body: Peter had to cross a literal threshold to share the gospel. Most barriers between people are social, not geographic: a lunch table, a neighborhood, a political tribe. Love has to walk through doors.
application.question: Whose home or table would cost you something socially to step into?

application.title: Closer than you think
application.body: Cornelius gathered relatives and friends and said they were all there to listen. He had prayed and given for years without knowing the full story. People around you may be nearer to faith than you assume.
application.question: Who in your life might already be seeking God and simply waiting for someone to explain?

context.heading: Who can stand in God's way?
context.body: Peter asks, "Who was I to hinder (kōlyein) the work of God?" The verb runs like a thread through Acts. The eunuch asks what prevents his baptism (8:36), and Peter asks who can withhold water (10:47). Luke's final word in the book is the related adverb "without hindrance" (28:31). No human barrier stops the gospel.

context.heading: Speaking to Greeks
context.body: Some believers from Cyprus and Cyrene began speaking "to the Greeks as well" in Antioch. Ancient manuscripts differ here between "Greeks" and "Hellenists," but the contrast with v. 19, where others spoke "only to Jews," shows Luke means non-Jews. This was a bold, unplanned outreach, and Antioch became the base of Paul's missions.

context.heading: Famine across the empire
context.body: Agabus predicts a severe famine over "the whole world" (oikoumenē), the inhabited world under Rome. Roman writers record repeated food shortages under Claudius (AD 41–54). Josephus describes a severe famine in Judea in the mid-40s, when Queen Helena of Adiabene bought grain from Egypt for Jerusalem. Luke's note fits what we know.

theology.title: Repentance is a gift
theology.body: The Jerusalem believers conclude, "God has granted even the Gentiles repentance unto life" (v. 18). Repentance is something God gives, not only something people produce (5:31; 2 Timothy 2:25). That means no one is beyond His reach, and no one who repents has grounds to boast.

theology.title: The hand of the Lord
theology.body: In Antioch "the hand of the Lord was with them" (v. 21), an Old Testament phrase for God's active power (Exodus 13:3; Ezra 7:9). The apostles did not plan this growth. Unnamed believers spoke about Jesus, and God did what only He can do.

theology.title: One family across distance
theology.body: The Gentile-majority church in Antioch sends famine relief to Jewish believers in Judea (vv. 29–30). Those who received the gospel through Jerusalem now share material help in return, a pattern Paul later explains (Romans 15:26–27). Belonging to Christ creates real obligations across ethnic and geographic lines.

application.title: Tell it, don't fight it
application.body: Criticized for eating with Gentiles, Peter did not pull rank. He told what happened step by step and let the evidence speak. A clear account often does more than a heated argument.
application.question: In a current conflict, are you trying to win or trying to tell the truth clearly?

application.title: Nameless pioneers
application.body: The church in Antioch began with believers whose names Luke never records. Great movements of God often start with ordinary people talking to their neighbors. You do not need a title to be used.
application.question: Which neighbor, coworker or classmate could you talk with about Jesus without waiting for permission?

application.title: Giving that fits your means
application.body: Each disciple gave according to their ability. No one was shamed for giving little, and no one was excused from giving. Generosity scaled to what you have is still real generosity.
application.question: Is your giving shaped by your actual ability, or by habit and whatever happens to be left over?

context.heading: Sixteen soldiers for one fisherman
context.body: Herod hands Peter over to four tetradia, "squads of four" soldiers, sixteen men rotating through the night watches. Two were chained to him and two guarded the door (v. 6). Herod likely knew Peter had slipped out of prison before (5:19). The heavier the guard, the plainer it becomes that the rescue was God's doing.

context.heading: "It must be his angel"
context.body: When Rhoda insists Peter is at the gate, the believers say it must be his angelos. Some Jews of the time believed a person had a guardian angel who could resemble them (compare Matthew 18:10). Luke reports the belief without explaining it. The irony is sharp: they found an angel easier to believe than an answered prayer.

context.heading: A tyrant's death
context.body: Herod is struck down and becomes skōlēkobrōtos, "eaten by worms." Ancient writers described such deaths for rulers who defied heaven, as in the account of Antiochus Epiphanes (2 Maccabees 9:9). Josephus adds that Agrippa wore a shimmering silver robe when the crowd hailed him as a god, and died after five days of agony.

theology.title: One taken, one rescued
theology.body: James is executed and Peter is freed (vv. 2, 7–11). Luke does not explain why God lets one apostle die and delivers another, and Scripture leaves such secrets with God (Deuteronomy 29:29). Both men were equally loved. Faith rests on God's character when His choices go unexplained.

theology.title: An exodus at Passover
theology.body: Peter is arrested during the Feast of Unleavened Bread (v. 3) and freed by night. The angel tells him to dress, put on his sandals and follow, echoing Israel's hurried departure from Egypt (Exodus 12:11). Peter says the Lord rescued him from Herod's grasp (v. 11), as God once rescued Israel from Pharaoh's hand (Exodus 18:10).

theology.title: God will not share His glory
theology.body: Herod accepts the shout, "This is the voice of a god, not a man!" and is struck down "because he did not give glory to God" (vv. 22–23). The LORD says He will not give His glory to another (Isaiah 42:8). Like Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 4:30–33), a king who claims divine honor is brought low, while the word of God keeps growing.

application.title: Praying without expecting
application.body: The church prayed earnestly for Peter, then told Rhoda she was out of her mind when he knocked. We can pray sincerely and still be startled when God answers. Expectation is part of faith.
application.question: What are you praying for that you would honestly be shocked to see answered?

application.title: Asleep between soldiers
application.body: Peter slept so soundly the night before his likely execution that the angel had to strike him to wake him. Peace like that comes from knowing whose hands your life is in. Anxiety often shows whose hands we think hold our future.
application.question: What keeps you awake at night, and whose hands do you really believe it is in?

application.title: Applause can kill
application.body: Herod fell at the height of his popularity. Praise is not wrong, but drinking it in as if you deserve worship is deadly. Status at work or online can quietly train us to expect applause.
application.question: How do you react inside when people praise you, and what does that reveal?

context.heading: Temple service in a Gentile city
context.body: The Antioch leaders were leitourgountōn, "ministering" or "worshiping," before the Lord. The Greek Old Testament uses the word for priests and Levites serving at the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 28:35; Numbers 18:2), and English "liturgy" comes from it. Here a diverse group, including a man from Cyrene and a childhood companion of Herod Antipas (v. 1), offers priestly worship far from Jerusalem.

context.heading: A governor and his magician
context.body: Sergius Paulus was proconsul of Cyprus, then a province governed for the Senate, and Luke gives him the correct title. Inscriptions mention Roman officials named Sergius Paullus in this period, though it is debated whether any is the same man. Roman elites often kept astrologers and magicians as advisers, so Bar-Jesus had a position to protect.

context.heading: Appointed for eternal life
context.body: Luke writes that all who were tetagmenoi, "appointed," for eternal life believed. Tassō means to arrange or assign, often in an official or military sense. Reformed readers see God's prior choice behind faith here. Others, including many Arminian readers, stress that God's purpose and human faith work together. Both agree Luke credits salvation to God while recording a real response of belief.

theology.title: Faithful through Israel's story
theology.body: Paul's synagogue sermon retells Israel's history: chosen ancestors, the exodus, the land, the judges, Saul and then David, "a man after My own heart" (v. 22). God had promised David a descendant who would reign forever (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Paul announces that God kept that promise by bringing Israel a Savior, Jesus (v. 23).

theology.title: Promises made sure by resurrection
theology.body: Paul quotes Isaiah 55:3 and Psalm 16:10: God will give "the holy and sure blessings promised to David" and will not let His Holy One see decay (vv. 34–35). David died and decayed; the one God raised did not (vv. 36–37). The resurrection is God's guarantee that His covenant promises cannot fail.

theology.title: A light for the nations
theology.body: When the synagogue leaders turn against them, Paul and Barnabas quote Isaiah 49:6: "I have made you a light for the Gentiles" (v. 47). In Isaiah the Servant is the light, and the apostles share in His mission. From the beginning, God's plan through Israel included the ends of the earth.

application.title: Mission born in worship
application.body: The first missionary journey did not start in a strategy session but while leaders were worshiping and fasting. Major direction came out of attention to God. Packed calendars rarely leave room to hear Him.
application.question: What would you have to cut from your week to actually listen before your next big decision?

application.title: Letting someone pass you
application.body: At the start it is "Barnabas and Saul"; soon it is "Paul and Barnabas." The senior partner seems to have let the younger man lead without complaint. Humility looks like celebrating someone else's rise.
application.question: Whose growing influence do you find hard to celebrate?

application.title: Shake off the dust
application.body: Driven out of Pisidian Antioch, Paul and Barnabas shook the dust off their feet and moved on, and the disciples were filled with joy. Faithfulness does not mean forcing a hearing where you have been clearly refused. Sometimes obedience means leaving well.
application.question: Where are you exhausting yourself trying to win people who have plainly said no?

context.heading: Empty gods
context.body: Paul urges the crowd to turn from these mataia, "worthless" or "empty" things, to the living God. The word describes what is futile and without substance. Old Testament writers mocked idols as lifeless objects that cannot speak, walk or save (Jeremiah 10:3–5). Paul uses that biblical critique on the gods of Lystra.

context.heading: Rain as testimony
context.body: God has not left Himself amartyros, "without testimony." Rain, fruitful seasons and food that fills hearts with gladness are His witness to people who never had the Scriptures (compare Romans 1:20). Speaking to farmers in rural Lycaonia, Paul begins with the God who sends rain, not with Moses or the prophets.

context.heading: A door God opened
context.body: Back in Syrian Antioch they report how God "had opened the door (thyra) of faith to the Gentiles." Paul later uses door language for opportunities to preach (1 Corinthians 16:9; Colossians 4:3). The stress falls on who opened it. The mission was God's before it was theirs.

theology.title: The living Creator
theology.body: Paul points the crowd to "the living God, who made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them" (v. 15), echoing Exodus 20:11 and Psalm 146:6. The true God is not one power among many, like Zeus or Hermes, but the maker of all. He cannot be flattered with sacrifices or confused with human beings.

theology.title: Patient with the nations
theology.body: In past generations God "let all nations go their own way" (v. 16). Paul does not mean God approved, but that He held back final judgment (17:30; Romans 3:25). His goodness in rain and harvest was meant to lead people toward Him (Romans 2:4).

theology.title: Power in battered messengers
theology.body: Paul is stoned, dragged out of town and left for dead, then gets up and walks back into the city (vv. 19–20). He later recalls this stoning (2 Corinthians 11:25) and says God's power is perfected in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). God advances His mission through wounded people, not invincible ones.

application.title: When people want to exalt you
application.body: The crowd tried to treat Paul and Barnabas as gods, and the two men tore their clothes in horror. Most of us are tempted in smaller ways, enjoying admiration that belongs to God. Refusing it takes deliberate effort.
application.question: Where do people treat you as more important than you are, and do you correct them?

application.title: Start where your listener lives
application.body: To farmers, Paul spoke of rain, crops and joy before anything else. He met them in the world they knew and pointed them to its Maker. Good witness begins with what your listener already sees.
application.question: What everyday experience in a friend's life could open an honest conversation about God?

application.title: Go back to the hard place
application.body: After being stoned at Lystra, Paul returned there to strengthen the new believers. Courage is often less about one dramatic moment and more about going back. Those young disciples needed to see the gospel was worth the bruises.
application.question: Where do you need to return after a painful experience, for the sake of someone else's faith?

context.heading: A yoke on the neck
context.body: Peter calls the demand that Gentiles keep the law a zygos ("yoke") that neither they nor their ancestors could bear. Jewish teachers spoke warmly of taking on the yoke of the Torah or of the kingdom. Peter is not mocking the law but denying that it can save. Jesus offered a different yoke: "My yoke is easy" (Matthew 11:29–30).

context.heading: Rebuilding David's tent
context.body: James quotes Amos 9:11–12, largely following the Greek translation: God will rebuild David's fallen tent so that the rest of humanity may seek the Lord, including Gentiles called by His name. James sees the risen Son of David and the Gentiles' faith as that promise coming true. The Hebrew of Amos 9:12 reads differently, and scholars discuss how James's use relates to it.

context.heading: The language of official decrees
context.body: The letter says, "It seemed good (edoxen) to the Holy Spirit and to us." Greek city councils announced decisions with the formula "it seemed good to the council and the people." The apostles use familiar civic language but name the Spirit as the senior partner. Their decision came through Scripture, testimony and debate, confirmed by the Spirit.

theology.title: The God who knows hearts
theology.body: Peter calls God "who knows the heart" (v. 8), a single Greek title the apostles also used when praying over Matthias (1:24). God saw faith in Gentile hearts and confirmed it by giving the Spirit. He does not need outward marks to know who is His (1 Samuel 16:7).

theology.title: A people for His name
theology.body: James says God has taken from the Gentiles "a people to be His own" (v. 14). "People" (laos) was the Old Testament word for Israel as God's treasured possession. Now Gentiles are included without becoming Jews, as the prophets foresaw (Zechariah 2:11). The family is wider than Jerusalem expected, yet it continues the story God began with Israel.

theology.title: Freedom shaped by love
theology.body: The council will not burden Gentiles with circumcision, yet asks them to avoid food offered to idols, blood, strangled meat and sexual immorality (vv. 20, 29). Freedom in Christ does not cancel holiness or concern for other believers' consciences. Paul works out the same balance in 1 Corinthians 8–10 and Romans 14.

application.title: Disagree in the open
application.body: The church faced a serious dispute and handled it with open debate, testimony and Scripture. The decision was written down and explained warmly to those affected. Hard issues in a family or church get worse when handled only through side conversations.
application.question: What disagreement around you needs an honest, structured conversation instead of quiet resentment?

application.title: Nothing added to grace
application.body: Some believers wanted Gentiles to earn their place through circumcision. We still add requirements: a style of worship, a political view, a level of polish. The gospel needs no extras.
application.question: What unwritten requirement do you expect people to meet before you fully accept them as fellow Christians?

application.title: Even good partners split
application.body: Paul and Barnabas disagreed so sharply over Mark that they parted ways, and Scripture does not hide it. God used both teams. Years later Paul wrote that Mark was useful to him (2 Timothy 4:11).
application.question: Who is someone you parted ways with that you could speak well of today?

context.heading: A little Rome in Macedonia
context.body: Philippi was a kolōnia, a Roman colony settled with army veterans after the civil wars of 42 and 31 BC. Colonies copied Rome's laws and government, and citizens prized their Roman status. That explains the charge that Paul and Silas promote customs unlawful "for us Romans" (v. 21). Paul later reminds the Philippians that their citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20).

context.heading: A spirit of python
context.body: The slave girl had a "spirit of divination," literally a spirit of pythōn. In Greek myth the Python was the serpent of Delphi slain by Apollo, and the name came to be linked with Apollo's oracle and with soothsayers. Her owners profited from her fortune-telling. She spoke truly about Paul's message, but he would not accept that source as a witness.

context.heading: Roman citizens beaten without trial
context.body: Paul reveals that he and Silas are Roman citizens who were beaten publicly without a trial. Roman law protected citizens from such treatment, and officials who ignored it risked serious trouble. Paul's demand for a public escort likely protected the young church, showing its founders were not criminals.

theology.title: Guided by closed doors
theology.body: The Holy Spirit keeps them from preaching in Asia, and "the Spirit of Jesus" will not let them enter Bithynia (vv. 6–7). Only then does the vision of the man from Macedonia come. The striking title "Spirit of Jesus" ties the Spirit closely to the risen Son. God guides through refusals as well as invitations.

theology.title: Whole households: where Christians differ
theology.body: Lydia's household is baptized (v. 15), and the jailer is baptized "with all his household" (v. 33), which rejoices that it had come to believe (v. 34). Christians who baptize infants see covenant households here. Those who baptize believers only note that the jailer's household heard the word and believed. All agree the gospel gathered whole families into God's people.

theology.title: Praise in the dark
theology.body: Bleeding and in stocks, Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns at midnight (v. 25). The Psalms are full of praise sung in distress: "At midnight I rise to give You thanks" (Psalm 119:62; compare 42:8). The God of Israel is worthy of praise before the rescue, not only after it.

application.title: Three unlikely first members
application.body: A wealthy businesswoman, an exploited slave girl and a Roman jailer: the church in Philippi began with people who would never have shared a table. The gospel forms a family across class and status. That is still one of its clearest signs.
application.question: Who in your church is most unlike you, and when did you last share a meal with them?

application.title: Freedom has enemies
application.body: The owners were not angry about theology but about lost income. When someone's freedom costs another person money, expect resistance. Exploitation often hides behind respectable business.
application.question: Does any of your income or convenience quietly depend on someone else's harm?

application.title: Songs before the earthquake
application.body: Paul and Silas sang before the doors opened, not after. Their praise did not wait for circumstances to change. Your worst night can still hold worship.
application.question: What would it look like to praise God in the situation that feels most like a prison right now?

context.heading: Turning the world upside down
context.body: The mob in Thessalonica says these men have anastatōsantes the world, "turned it upside down." The verb was used for stirring up revolt; Luke uses it later of an Egyptian rebel (21:38). The real accusation is political: they proclaim "another king, named Jesus" (v. 7), against Caesar's decrees. In a city loyal to Rome, that was dangerous talk.

context.heading: A seed-picking babbler
context.body: Some philosophers call Paul a spermologos, "babbler," literally a "seed-picker," like a bird pecking up scraps in the market. It was slang for someone who collects scraps of ideas and repeats them without understanding. Others think he is promoting foreign gods. Some scholars suggest they heard "Jesus" and "Anastasis" (resurrection) as a pair of new deities.

context.heading: Quoting their own poets
context.body: Paul quotes lines his audience knew. "In Him we live and move and have our being" is often traced to the Cretan poet Epimenides. "We are His offspring" comes from Aratus, a poet from Paul's home region of Cilicia, with a similar line in a Stoic hymn by Cleanthes. Paul uses what their poets glimpsed to point to the Creator they did not know.

theology.title: The God who needs nothing
theology.body: God made the world, is Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in shrines made by hands and is not served as if He needed anything (vv. 24–25). He is the one who gives everyone life and breath (Isaiah 42:5). Against carved idols and the distant gods of the Epicureans, Paul presents the God of Genesis 1: self-sufficient, near and generous.

theology.title: Nations placed on purpose
theology.body: From one man God made every nation and set their times and boundaries so that people would seek Him (vv. 26–27; Deuteronomy 32:8). Human history is not random. The variety of peoples comes from one ancestor and serves one purpose, and God is not far from any of us.

theology.title: A day already set
theology.body: God overlooked past ignorance but now commands all people everywhere to repent, because He has fixed a day to judge the world through the man He appointed (vv. 30–31). The proof He gives is the resurrection. For Greeks who often saw the body as something to escape, a raised body was the hardest claim to accept (v. 32).

application.title: Let distress become conversation
application.body: Paul was deeply troubled by a city full of idols, and his distress sent him to the marketplace to talk with anyone there. Complaining about culture is easy and changes little. Paul's grief became engagement.
application.question: What troubles you about your culture, and where could that turn into a real conversation this week?

application.title: Learn what your neighbors read
application.body: Paul knew Greek poetry well enough to quote it from memory. He took his audience's ideas seriously enough to find common ground and then challenge it. Understanding what your friends watch, read and believe earns you a hearing.
application.question: What does the person you most want to reach care about, and how well do you actually understand it?

application.title: Mixed results are normal
application.body: In Athens some sneered, some wanted to hear more, and a few believed, including Dionysius and a woman named Damaris. That is not failure. Faithfulness is measured by the message given, not by the response received.
application.question: Have you gone quiet about your faith because the last response was not what you hoped?

context.heading: Gripped by the word
context.body: When Silas and Timothy arrive, Paul "devoted himself fully" to the word. The verb synechō means to hold fast or press hard, as if the message had a grip on him. Many think the two brought a gift from the Macedonian churches (2 Corinthians 11:9; Philippians 4:15), freeing Paul to set aside tentmaking and preach full time.

context.heading: A vow at Cenchreae
context.body: At Cenchreae, Corinth's eastern port, Paul has his head shaved to keep a vow. It was probably a vow similar to the Nazirite vow, in which a person let their hair grow for a set time and then cut it (Numbers 6:5, 18), though the details are debated. Paul still freely practiced Jewish forms of devotion, not to earn salvation but as worship.

context.heading: An eloquent Alexandrian
context.body: Apollos is logios, "eloquent" or "learned," a word for someone trained in speech and literature. Alexandria in Egypt was a great center of learning with a large Jewish community, home to the Jewish philosopher Philo. Apollos knew the Scriptures well but knew only John's baptism. Later some in Corinth rallied around him as their favorite teacher (1 Corinthians 1:12; 3:4–6).

theology.title: People He already calls His
theology.body: The Lord tells Paul not to be afraid, "because I have many people in this city" (v. 10). Corinth was notorious, yet God already counted people there as His before they had believed. Like Elijah's hidden seven thousand (1 Kings 19:18), God's people are more than His servants can see. Christians relate this to election in different ways, but its comfort to weary workers is plain.

theology.title: Protection through an indifferent judge
theology.body: Gallio dismisses the case as a quarrel about words, names and Jewish law (vv. 14–15). His ruling, by a senior Roman official, effectively treated the Christians as part of Judaism for the moment, giving Paul room to work. God keeps His promise that no one will harm Paul (v. 10) through a pagan who did not care either way.

theology.title: The Christ of the Scriptures
theology.body: Paul in Corinth and Apollos in Achaia both reason from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ (vv. 5, 28). The Messiah is not a Christian invention but the one Israel's Scriptures promised (Luke 24:44). The God who spoke through the prophets now speaks through their fulfillment.

application.title: Brave people feel fear
application.body: Paul, the great apostle, needed the Lord to tell him, "Do not be afraid; keep on speaking." Courageous people are not fearless; they keep going while afraid. Fear tempts us more often toward silence than toward running away.
application.question: Where has fear made you go quiet, even though you have not walked away?

application.title: A household that travels
application.body: Priscilla and Aquila lost their home in Rome, rebuilt in Corinth, then moved again to Ephesus. Wherever they went, their home and trade served the gospel. A household can be a base for ministry anywhere.
application.question: How could your home, exactly as it is now, serve someone's faith this month?

application.title: Correct in private
application.body: When Priscilla and Aquila heard Apollos teach something incomplete, they took him aside rather than correcting him in front of others. That protected his dignity and strengthened his ministry. Private correction is usually more loving and more effective.
application.question: When someone you respect gets something wrong, do you go to them or talk about them?

context.heading: A rented lecture hall
context.body: Paul moves his daily teaching to the scholē ("lecture hall") of Tyrannus. Scholē first meant "leisure," the free time used for learning, and gives us the word "school." One early manuscript adds that Paul taught from about 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., the hot midday rest when the hall was free. If so, he likely worked at his trade in the cooler hours (20:34).

context.heading: Exorcists using a borrowed name
context.body: Traveling Jewish exorkistai, "exorcists," try the formula "Jesus, whom Paul proclaims." Magical texts from this period pile up the names of gods, angels and even Israel's God, assuming the right name gives control. Jesus' name is not a spell. The spirit knows Jesus and Paul but not these men, and they flee naked and wounded.

context.heading: Guardian of Artemis
context.body: The city clerk calms the crowd by reminding them that Ephesus is the neōkoros, "guardian of the temple," of Artemis. The title, literally "temple sweeper," was an official honor cities competed for, and Ephesian coins and inscriptions proudly display it. The clerk also fears Roman officials will treat the riot as sedition (v. 40).

theology.title: The word outmuscles magic
theology.body: After the scrolls are burned, Luke writes that the word of the Lord "powerfully continued to spread and prevail" (v. 20). In a city famous for magic and for Artemis, God's word proves stronger than both. The Lord is greater than every rival power, seen or unseen.

theology.title: Power without relationship fails
theology.body: God works extraordinary miracles through Paul (v. 11), yet the sons of Sceva discover that His power cannot be borrowed by people who do not know Him. Jesus warned that some would use His name and still hear, "I never knew you" (Matthew 7:22–23). God's power flows through relationship, not formula.

theology.title: Handmade gods are no gods
theology.body: Demetrius complains that Paul says "man-made gods are no gods at all" (v. 26), echoing Isaiah 44:9–20 and Psalm 115:4–8. The silversmiths grasped what the rioting crowd missed: the living God threatens every idol, including profitable ones. Belief in Him reshapes economies as well as hearts.

application.title: A clean, public break
application.body: The new believers did not tuck their magic scrolls away in case they needed them later. They burned them publicly, at great cost. Some sins need a decisive, visible end rather than careful management.
application.question: What are you keeping around just in case that you need to get rid of for good?

application.title: Christian words as technique
application.body: The exorcists used Jesus' name without knowing Him and got hurt. It is possible to use prayers, verses and church habits as a method for getting good outcomes. God is not a tool.
application.question: Where are you using Christian language or habits to get results rather than to know Jesus?

application.title: Faith that touches the budget
application.body: Demetrius' guild felt the gospel in their profits. Real conversion changes how people earn, spend and buy. If your faith has never touched your finances, it may not have reached very deep.
application.question: What has following Jesus actually cost you financially, and what should it cost?

context.heading: Gathering on the first day
context.body: The believers in Troas come together "on the first day of the week" to break bread. This is one of the earliest hints that Christians met on Sunday, the day of the resurrection (1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10). They probably met in the evening after a workday, which explains the late hour, the many lamps and a drowsy young man in the window (vv. 8–9).

context.heading: Running to the finish
context.body: Paul wants only to finish his dromos, his "course" or race, like a runner on a track. He returns to the image near the end of his life: "I have finished the race" (2 Timothy 4:7). His goal is not to preserve his life but to complete the task Jesus gave him, testifying to the good news of God's grace.

context.heading: The whole will of God
context.body: Paul did not shrink from declaring "the whole will (boulē) of God." Boulē means plan, purpose or counsel. He taught the full sweep of God's purpose, not just the welcome parts, in public and from house to house (v. 20). That is why he can say he is innocent of everyone's blood, echoing the faithful watchman of Ezekiel 33:7–9.

theology.title: Bought with His own blood
theology.body: Paul calls the church the church of God, "which He purchased with His own blood" (v. 28). Many read this as a striking witness to Christ's full deity. Some manuscripts read "church of the Lord," and the Greek can also mean "with the blood of His own [Son]." On every reading, the church is precious because it cost the life of God's Son.

theology.title: Grace that keeps building
theology.body: Paul commits the elders "to God and to the word of His grace, which can build you up and give you an inheritance" (v. 32). The God who saved them by grace will also sustain them. Paul is leaving, but God and His word remain. Under-shepherds come and go; the chief Shepherd stays (1 Peter 5:4).

theology.title: Led into hardship with open eyes
theology.body: Paul goes to Jerusalem "compelled by the Spirit," while the Spirit warns him in every city that chains await (vv. 22–23). God does not promise him ease but prepares him for suffering. Jesus likewise set His face toward Jerusalem knowing what waited there (Luke 9:51).

application.title: Ministry with tears
application.body: Paul reminds the elders that he served them with humility and tears. Caring for people that never costs you emotionally may never have truly engaged them. Tears are not weakness in leadership.
application.question: Whom do you care about enough that their struggles have cost you tears?

application.title: Watch yourself first
application.body: Paul tells the elders to keep watch over themselves and then over the flock. Leaders who neglect their own hearts eventually harm the people they lead. The same holds for parents, managers and friends.
application.question: What warning signs in your own life have you been ignoring while you look after everyone else?

application.title: Give more than you take
application.body: Paul worked with his own hands to support himself, his companions and the weak. Many modern relationships are quietly transactional: networking, favors owed, likes returned. Paul's model runs the other way.
application.question: In which relationship are you mostly taking, and what would giving look like there?

context.heading: A prophet acts it out
context.body: Agabus takes Paul's zōnē ("belt"), ties his own hands and feet and says the owner will be bound in Jerusalem. Old Testament prophets often acted out their messages: Isaiah walked barefoot (Isaiah 20:2–4), Jeremiah ruined a linen belt (Jeremiah 13:1–11), and Ezekiel lay on his side (Ezekiel 4:4–8). The prophecy predicts chains; it does not forbid the journey.

context.heading: Paying for a purification
context.body: James asks Paul to purify himself (hagnisthēti) with four men completing a vow and to pay their expenses. Ending a Nazirite vow required several offerings for each person (Numbers 6:13–20), so covering the cost was a generous, public act of devotion. Paul could do this in good conscience, having become like a Jew to win Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20).

context.heading: A wall with a death warning
context.body: The crowd claims Paul brought Greeks into the temple. A low barrier separated the Court of the Gentiles from the inner courts, and posted inscriptions in Greek and Latin warned that any foreigner who passed it would be put to death. One such Greek inscription survives today. Paul later wrote that Christ has torn down the dividing wall of hostility (Ephesians 2:14).

theology.title: "The Lord's will be done"
theology.body: When the believers cannot change Paul's mind, they say, "The Lord's will be done" (v. 14), echoing Jesus in Gethsemane (Luke 22:42). Like his Master, Paul goes up to Jerusalem knowing suffering awaits. God's will is not always the safe path, and godly people can weigh His warnings differently.

theology.title: Daughters who prophesied
theology.body: Philip had four unmarried daughters who prophesied (v. 9), a fulfillment of Joel's promise that sons and daughters would prophesy (2:17). Christians differ on what prophecy looks like today and how it relates to teaching and leadership roles in the church. Luke plainly presents these women as Spirit-gifted servants honored among God's people.

theology.title: Patience over the law
theology.body: Thousands of Jewish believers still keep the law zealously (v. 20), while the elders reaffirm that Gentile believers are not bound by it (v. 25). The God who gave the law fulfilled it in Christ, and the church needed time to work out what that meant for Jewish practice. Acts models patience and room for difference on this question, not one rule pressed on everyone.

application.title: When people who love you object
application.body: Paul's friends wept and begged him not to go, and he said they were breaking his heart. Both sides loved Jesus and each other, and they disagreed. Faithfulness sometimes means hearing loving warnings fully and still following what God has made clear.
application.question: How do you tell the difference between a loving warning and a pull toward compromise?

application.title: Answer the rumor
application.body: Many Jewish believers had heard that Paul told Jews to abandon Moses, and it was false. The elders did not shrug it off; they asked Paul to take a costly step to answer it. Your reputation matters for the sake of the gospel.
application.question: What misunderstanding about you could you take one concrete step to correct?

application.title: Bend where you can
application.body: Paul paid for other men's purification rites to build trust with Jewish believers. He gave up his preferences without giving up the gospel. Flexibility on secondary things is a gift to unity.
application.question: Where could you set aside a preference for the sake of peace with fellow believers?

context.heading: Washing away sins
context.body: Ananias tells Paul to be baptized and "wash your sins away (apolousai), calling on His name." The verb means to wash off completely and appears only here and in 1 Corinthians 6:11. Many evangelicals tie the cleansing to calling on the Lord, with baptism as its outward sign. Other traditions see baptism itself as a means God uses to cleanse. All agree it is the Lord who removes sin.

context.heading: The Roman scourge
context.body: The commander orders Paul examined by flogging. The noun is mastix, the Roman scourge: leather straps weighted with bone or metal, used to force confessions from non-citizens. It could cripple or kill. Paul had been beaten with rods before (16:22), but this was worse, and his citizenship spares him.

context.heading: Citizenship for sale
context.body: The commander says he paid a high price for his citizenship. Roman historians report that under Emperor Claudius citizenship could be bought through bribes to officials. New citizens often took the emperor's name, and the commander is Claudius Lysias (23:26). Paul was born a citizen, which gave him higher standing than the officer in charge.

theology.title: Same story, new audience
